rv.q: Pinnock really has made this story of soiled inheritance, unrecorded Black histories and racial appropriation an enjoyable experience.
Cromwell’s production has a hectic energy designed to carry us over the flaws.
It is a compelling piece that mixes wry wit with real bite, even if the campness of Miranda Cromwell's staging is a little erratic.
Unfortunately, Winsome Pinnock offers a silly play about a serious subject, as the long shadow of slavery is cast upon a modern-day country house.
The three actors do their very best to keep The Authenticator on course, but in the end it's a lost cause.
As a tense, talky, quietly incendiary three-hander about race, legacy and intellectual power, it cuts deeper than any jump scare.

THE AUTHENTICATOR directed by Miranda Cromwell, shines a light on Britain’s colonial, slave-owning past, while also managing to instil a creepy air to proceedings resulting in a gently amusing caper imbued with serious social and historic undertones.
And yet, it is this awkward juxtaposition that becomes The Authenticator’s true strength.
It’s rather unsatisfying, then, for theatregoers looking to be startled.
But perhaps because it’s all played so lightly, it’s unclear what it’s looking to say.

Stories about slavery tend to be simplistic: white perpetrators are bad, black victims good. One of the more striking features of Winsome Pinnock’s new play, The Authenticator, is her insistence that reality is always more complicated.
The Authenticator is a pacy and surprisingly witty three-hander which explores the legacy of enslavement for both those who were responsible and those who are descendants of the enslaved.
It is complex, compelling and quietly devastating.
The jewel in its crown is the serious message uncovered, and told with refreshing humour, leading to the perfect balance.
With inventive staging, strong performances, and an engaging plot, it’s a compelling addition to the National Theatre’s current season.
But it feels oddly lazy for the NT: as if any play about the disgrace and misery of the slave trade gets a free pass, exempt from any rigour in playbuilding, character and probability.

cn.t: Pinnock's witty, atmospheric play tackles Britain's slavery legacy through a gothic country-house mystery. Critics praise its humor and thought-provoking complexity, though some find it tonally erratic with excessive exposition.
